# ArkRegex

> Regular expressions with inferred types

# Overview

> Install ArkRegex and see what it infers from the strings you already pass to new RegExp().

`regex` takes the same arguments as `new RegExp()` and returns a `RegExp` typed with the strings it matches, its captures and its flags:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

const ok = regex("^ok$", "i")
// const ok: Regex<"ok" | "oK" | "Ok" | "OK", {
//     flags: "i";
// }>

const date = regex("^(\\d{4})-(\\d{2})-(\\d{2})$")
// const date: Regex<`${number}-${number}-${number}`, {
//     captures: [`${number}`, `${number}`, `${number}`];
// }>
```

`.exec()` returns typed captures:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

const date = regex("^(?<year>\\d{4})-(?<month>\\d{2})$")

const match = date.exec("2026-10")

if (match) {
	const month = match.groups.month
	// const month: `${number}`
}
```

At runtime, `regex(src, flags)` is `new RegExp(src, flags)`. The result is a plain `RegExp`, and `Regex` exists only in your types, so the package adds one function to your bundle.

## Installation

```bash
npm install arkregex
```

Performs best with TypeScript 5.9 or later, including TypeScript 7.

If you're upgrading, [Upgrading](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#arkregex) lists what changed in inference.

## Features

- **Types**: infers the strings an expression matches, its positional and named captures and its flags. See [Inference](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/inference).
- **Syntax**: parses the syntax `new RegExp()` accepts, including named groups, lookarounds, backreferences, modifiers and Unicode properties. A few valid patterns are rejected and a few invalid ones aren't caught; see [what isn't checked](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/errors#what-isnt-checked).
- **Errors**: mistakes like an unclosed group or a reference to a group that doesn't exist are [type errors](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/errors).
- **No runtime cost**: the only code that runs is `new RegExp()`.

## Syntax highlighting

The [ArkType extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=arktypeio.arkdark) highlights the expression inside `regex` calls.

## ArkType

`arktype` re-exports `regex` and the `Regex` type, so if you use ArkType you don't need to install `arkregex` separately:

```ts
import { regex, type Regex } from "arktype"
```

ArkType also uses ArkRegex to infer its own regex literals, so `type("/^\\d{5}$/")` infers ``Type<`${number}`>``. See [ArkType](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/arktype).

# Inference

> The type ArkRegex infers for each part of a regular expression.

Each `Regex` carries the strings it matches, its captures and its flags. Where an exact type would be impractical, ArkRegex widens to `string` or `` `${number}` ``, so the inferred type is meant to include every string the expression matches. A few patterns currently infer a narrower type than that; they're listed under [known gaps](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/faq#known-gaps).

| Syntax | Infers |
| - | - |
| `abc` | `"abc"` |
| no `^` or `$` | the type padded with `` `${string}` `` on that side |
| `a\|b` | `"a" \| "b"` |
| `?`, `{2}`, `{2,3}` | every allowed repetition |
| `+`, `{2,}` | the required repetitions followed by `` `${string}` `` |
| `*` | `""`, or one repetition followed by `` `${string}` `` |
| `\d`, `[0-9]` | `` `${number}` `` |
| `[abc]` | `"a" \| "b" \| "c"` |
| `.`, `\w`, `\W`, `\s`, `\S`, `\D`, `\p{…}`, `[^…]`, ranges like `[a-z]` | `string` |
| `\b`, `\B`, `(?=…)`, `(?!…)`, `(?<=…)`, `(?<!…)` | nothing |
| `(…)`, `(?<name>…)` | the group's type, plus a capture |
| `\1`, `\k<name>` | whatever the referenced group matched |
| `(?i:…)`, `(?-i:…)` | the letters inside with or without their case variants |
| an escaped character like `\.` | the character itself |

Lazy quantifiers like `+?` infer the same type as their greedy versions.

## Anchors

An expression without `^` or `$` can match anywhere in a string, so its type is padded with `` `${string}` ``:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

const unanchored = regex("abc")
// const unanchored: Regex<`${string}abc${string}`, {}>

const anchored = regex("^abc$")
// const anchored: Regex<"abc", {}>
```

## Unions

```ts
const color = regex("^(red|green|blue)$")
// const color: Regex<"red" | "green" | "blue", {
//     captures: ["red"] | ["blue"] | ["green"];
// }>
```

A branch can be empty:

```ts
const signed = regex("^(-|)1$")
// const signed: Regex<"1" | "-1", {
//     captures: ["-"] | [""];
// }>
```

## Quantifiers

Bounded quantifiers expand into every allowed repetition, so a large bound like `{0,60}` produces a union of 61 strings:

```ts
const range = regex("^a{2,3}$")
// const range: Regex<"aa" | "aaa", {}>

const optional = regex("^colou?r$")
// const optional: Regex<"color" | "colour", {}>
```

Unbounded quantifiers keep the required repetitions and end in `` `${string}` ``. A `*` can also match nothing, so it adds `""`:

```ts
const atLeastTwo = regex("^a{2,}$")
// const atLeastTwo: Regex<`aa${string}`, {}>

const zeroOrMore = regex("^a*$")
// const zeroOrMore: Regex<"" | `a${string}`, {}>
```

A bounded run of digits becomes `` `${number}` ``, plus `""` if it can repeat zero times. An unbounded run like `\d+` becomes `string`, since a long enough run of digits isn't a finite number:

```ts
const version = regex("^(\\d{1,3})\\.(\\d{1,3})$")
// const version: Regex<`${number}.${number}`, {
//     captures: [`${number}`, `${number}`];
// }>

const short = regex("^\\d{0,3}$")
// const short: Regex<`${number}` | "", {}>

const digits = regex("^\\d+$")
// const digits: Regex<string, {}>
```

## Character sets

A set of literal characters becomes a union of them, and a digit range becomes `` `${number}` ``. Any other range widens to `string`, since listing its characters would produce large unions:

```ts
const abc = regex("^[abc]$")
// const abc: Regex<"a" | "b" | "c", {}>

const digit = regex("^[0-9]$")
// const digit: Regex<`${number}`, {}>

const hex = regex("^[0-9a-f]+$")
// const hex: Regex<string, {}>
```

Negated sets like `[^abc]` and classes like `.`, `\w`, `\s` and `\p{L}` also widen to `string`.

## Escapes

Write a regex escape like `\d` or `\.` with two backslashes in a JS string, and a character a JS string can represent itself, like a newline or `é`, with one. An escaped character infers as itself:

```ts
const price = regex("^\\$\\d+\\.\\d{2}$")
// const price: Regex<`$${string}.${number}`, {}>

const tab = regex("^a\tb$")
// const tab: Regex<"a\tb", {}>
```

Writing `"\\n"` where `"\n"` would do is an [error](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/errors#escapes).

## Captures

Positional captures are inferred as a tuple. A group that may not participate in a match captures `undefined`:

```ts
const maybeB = regex("^a(b)?$")
// const maybeB: Regex<"a" | "ab", {
//     captures: ["b"] | [undefined];
// }>
```

Captures are correlated with the branch that matched. A group in a branch that didn't match is `undefined`, so each tuple lines up with what `.exec()` returns:

```ts
const ab = regex("^(?:(a)|(b))$")

type Captures = typeof ab.inferCaptures
// type Captures = [undefined, "b"] | ["a", undefined]
```

## Named captures

```ts
const date = regex("^(?<year>\\d{4})-(?<month>\\d{2})-(?<day>\\d{2})$")

type Names = typeof date.inferNamedCaptures
// type Names = {
//     year: `${number}`;
//     month: `${number}`;
//     day: `${number}`;
// }
```

Named captures are correlated across branches the same way:

```ts
const unit = regex("^(?:(?<px>\\d+)px|(?<em>\\d+)em)$")

type Names = typeof unit.inferNamedCaptures
// type Names = {
//     px: undefined;
//     em: string;
// } | {
//     px: string;
//     em: undefined;
// }
```

## Backreferences

A backreference matches the same string its group did, so it repeats that branch of the group's type:

```ts
const double = regex("^(a|b)\\1$")
// const double: Regex<"bb" | "aa", {
//     captures: ["a"] | ["b"];
// }>

const quoted = regex("^(?<q>'|\")x\\k<q>$")
// const quoted: Regex<"\"x\"" | "'x'", {
//     captures: ["'"] | ["\""];
//     names: {
//         q: "\"";
//     } | {
//         q: "'";
//     };
// }>
```

## Lookarounds

Lookarounds and word boundaries check a position without consuming characters, so they don't change the type:

```ts
const getter = regex("^get(?=[A-Z])\\w+$")
// const getter: Regex<`get${string}`, {}>
```

## Flags

Flags are inferred, and `i` expands every letter to both cases:

```ts
const ok = regex("^ok$", "i")
// const ok: Regex<"ok" | "oK" | "Ok" | "OK", {
//     flags: "i";
// }>
```

Flags must be written in alphabetical order (`"gi"`, not `"ig"`), the same order `RegExp#flags` returns them in. See [why](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/faq#why-is-my-flags-string-an-error).

Modifiers apply `i` to part of an expression, or remove it:

```ts
const title = regex("^(?i:a)b$")
// const title: Regex<"ab" | "Ab", {}>

const strict = regex("^(?-i:a)b$", "i")
// const strict: Regex<"ab" | "aB", {
//     flags: "i";
// }>
```

The `s` flag doesn't change inference, since `.` already infers `string`. The `m` flag is a [known gap](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/faq#known-gaps).

## `.test()`

`.test()` narrows its input to the expression's type:

```ts
const color = regex("^(red|green|blue)$")

declare const input: string

if (color.test(input)) {
	const narrowed = input
	// const narrowed: "red" | "green" | "blue"
}
```

Only rely on the `true` branch. In the `false` branch, TypeScript removes the whole inferred type from the input, which also removes strings that didn't match whenever the type was widened. See [known gaps](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/faq#known-gaps).

## `.exec()`

`.exec()` returns a typed match, including `groups` and, with the `d` flag, `indices`:

```ts
const date = regex("^(?<year>\\d{4})-(?<month>\\d{2})-(?<day>\\d{2})$", "d")

const match = date.exec("2026-10-07")

if (match) {
	const year = match.groups.year
	// const year: `${number}`

	const [start, end] = match.indices.groups.year
	// const start: number
}
```

Its type is [`inferExecArray`](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/types#regex).

# Errors

> Which mistakes in an expression are type errors, and which aren't checked.

If `regex` can't parse an expression, the argument is a type error with a message saying why:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

regex("a(b") // Missing )

regex("+a") // Quantifier + requires a preceding token

regex("(?<a>x)\\k<b>") // Group b does not exist
```

Most of these would also throw from `new RegExp()`. The rest are valid at runtime but rejected, usually because they're likely a mistake, like an anchor in the middle of a pattern. The others are listed under [what isn't checked](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/errors#what-isnt-checked).

| Message | Example | `new RegExp()` |
| - | - | - |
| `Missing )`, `Missing ]`, `Missing >` | `"a(b"` | throws |
| `Unmatched ) before b` | `"a)b"` | throws |
| `Quantifier + requires a preceding token` | `"+a"` | throws |
| `A regex cannot end with \` | `"a\\"` | throws |
| `Capture group <> requires a name` | `"(?<>a)"` | throws |
| `literal ? must be escaped at the start of a group` | `"(?i)"` | throws |
| `Modifier flag x must be 'i', 'm' or 's'` | `"(?x:a)"` | throws |
| `Modifier i cannot appear multiple times in a single group` | `"(?ii:a)"` | throws |
| `Modifiers can include at most one '-' to negate subsequent flags` | `"(?i-m-s:a)"` | throws |
| `- must be followed by the modifier flag to negate ('i', 'm' or 's')` | `"(?-:a)"` | throws |
| `Group b does not exist` | `"(?<a>x)\\k<b>"` | throws |
| `Group 2 does not exist` | `"(a)\\2"` | throws with `u` or `v`; otherwise `\2` is an octal escape |
| `\k must be followed by a named reference like <name>` | `"\\ka"` | throws with `u`, `v` or a named group; otherwise matches `ka` |
| `\p must be followed by a property like \p{Emoji_Presentation}` | `"\\p"` | throws with `u` or `v`; otherwise matches `p` |
| `Quantifier {1.5} must use natural numbers` | `"a{1.5}"` | throws with `u` or `v`; otherwise matches the text `a{1.5}` |
| `Escape preceding q is unnecessary and should be removed.` | `"\\q"` | throws with `u` or `v`; otherwise matches `q` |
| `Reference to incomplete group '1' has no effect` | `"(a\\1)"` | valid; the reference matches `""` |
| `Anchor ^ may not appear mid-pattern` | `"a^b"` | valid |
| `Empty character set [] is unsatisfiable` | `"[]"` | valid; never matches |
| `\n should be specified with a single backslash like regex('\n')` | `"\\n"` | valid |
| `\cX notation is not supported. Use hex (\x) or unicode (\u) instead.` | `"\\cJ"` | valid |

## Escapes

Escaping a character with no special meaning is an error, as is writing a character a JS string can represent itself with a regex escape. Write `"\n"`, `"\t"`, `"\x41"` or `"\u00e9"` with one backslash:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

regex("\\q") // Escape preceding q is unnecessary and should be removed.

regex("\\n") // \n should be specified with a single backslash like regex('\n')
```

## What isn't checked

Some valid patterns are rejected:

- `\cX` control escapes, and `\/`, which a string doesn't need (write `/`).
- `\}`, which the `u` and `v` flags require outside a character class. Write `[}]` instead.
- `^` or `$` in the middle of a pattern, even with the `m` flag.
- A reference to a group defined later, like `"\\k<a>(?<a>x)"`.
- Flags out of alphabetical order, like `"ig"`. Write `"gi"`.

Some patterns that `new RegExp()` throws on aren't caught:

- Ranges out of order, like `"[z-a]"`.
- Duplicate group names in the same branch, like `"(?<a>x)(?<a>y)"`.
- Syntax that only throws with the `u` or `v` flag, like `"\\-"`, `"\\p{Foo}"` or `"a{1,b}"`.

Quantifier bounds out of order, like `"a{2,1}"`, are an error, but only `Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite`.

The `v` flag's nested classes and set operations, like `[[a-z]--[aeiou]]`, aren't parsed. They aren't errors, but see [known gaps](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/faq#known-gaps).

## Escape hatch

To use a pattern ArkRegex rejects or can't infer, type it yourself with [`regex.as`](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/types#regexas).

# Types

> The Regex type and its members, plus regex.infer, regex.parse, regex.validate and regex.as.

## `Regex`

`regex()` returns a `RegExp` typed as `Regex<pattern, ctx>`, where `pattern` is the strings it matches and `ctx` is an object with optional `flags`, `captures` and `names`. `Regex` extends `RegExp`, so it can be passed anywhere a `RegExp` is expected.

| Member | Type |
| - | - |
| `infer` | `pattern` |
| `inferCaptures` | the positional captures as a tuple |
| `inferNamedCaptures` | the named captures as an object |
| `inferExecArray` | what `.exec()` returns on a match |
| `flags` | the flags string, like `"gi"` |
| `test(s)` | narrows `s` to `pattern` |
| `exec(s)` | `inferExecArray \| null` |

The `infer` members exist only in types: read them with `typeof`. At runtime they're `undefined`.

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

const date = regex("^(?<year>\\d{4})-(?<month>\\d{2})$")

type Pattern = typeof date.infer
// type Pattern = `${number}-${number}`

type Captures = typeof date.inferCaptures
// type Captures = [`${number}`, `${number}`]

type Names = typeof date.inferNamedCaptures
// type Names = {
//     year: `${number}`;
//     month: `${number}`;
// }
```

`Regex<pattern>` as a parameter type accepts any expression whose inferred type is assignable to `pattern`. A `Regex` with no arguments accepts any `regex()` result, but not a plain `RegExp`:

```ts
import { regex, type Regex } from "arkregex"

const majorMinor = (r: Regex<`${number}.${number}`>) => r

const version = regex("^(\\d{1,3})\\.(\\d{1,3})$")
const tag = regex("^v(\\d{1,3})$")

majorMinor(version)

majorMinor(tag) // Regex<`v${number}`, ...> is not assignable to Regex<`${number}.${number}`>
```

## `regex.infer`

Infers the pattern of an expression without creating one. An optional second argument passes flags:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

type Version = regex.infer<"^(\\d{1,3})\\.(\\d{1,3})$">
// type Version = `${number}.${number}`

type Ok = regex.infer<"^ok$", "i">
// type Ok = "OK" | "Ok" | "oK" | "ok"
```

## `regex.parse` and `regex.validate`

`regex.parse` gives the full `Regex` type, or the error message if the expression is invalid. `regex.validate` is the parameter type `regex` uses to report that message. Together they let you write your own wrappers:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

const anchored = <src extends string>(
	src: regex.validate<src>
): regex.parse<`^${src}$`> => regex.as(`^${src}$`) as never

const ab = anchored("a(b)")
// const ab: Regex<"ab", {
//     captures: ["b"];
// }>
```

## `regex.as`

If an expression is too long or complex for TypeScript to infer (e.g. you see `Type instantiation is excessively deep`), or uses syntax ArkRegex [rejects](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/errors#what-isnt-checked), type it yourself with `regex.as`. It skips parsing and validation entirely:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

const version = regex.as<`v${number}`, { captures: [`${number}`] }>("^v(\\d+)$")
// const version: Regex<`v${number}`, {
//     captures: [`${number}`];
// }>
```

The flags argument isn't read for types. If you pass flags, declare them in `ctx` too, so `.flags` and `.exec()` are typed to match:

```ts
const newline = regex.as<"\n", { flags: "g" }>("^\\cJ$", "g")
// const newline: Regex<"\n", {
//     flags: "g";
// }>
```

With no type arguments, `regex.as` returns `Regex<string>`.

# ArkType

> How ArkType infers its regex literals and accepts regex() values as definitions.

`arktype` uses ArkRegex to infer its regex literals, and re-exports `regex` and the `Regex` type, so there's nothing extra to install:

```ts
import { regex, type } from "arktype"

const ZipCode = type("/^\\d{5}$/")
// const ZipCode: Type<`${number}`, {}>
```

Like `new RegExp()`, a regex literal matches anywhere in a string unless you anchor it with `^` and `$`, and its type is padded to match:

```ts
const HasAbc = type("/abc/")
// const HasAbc: Type<`${string}abc${string}`, {}>
```

## Flags

A regex literal in a string definition can't have flags:

```ts
type("/^ok$/i") // 'i' is not allowed here
```

To use flags, pass a `regex()` value instead.

## `regex()` definitions

A `Regex` can be used directly as a definition, with or without flags:

```ts
const Ok = type(regex("^ok$", "i"))
// const Ok: Type<"ok" | "oK" | "Ok" | "OK", {}>

const Address = type({
	street: "string",
	zip: regex("^\\d{5}(-\\d{4})?$")
})

type Address = typeof Address.infer
// type Address = {
//     street: string;
//     zip: `${number}` | `${number}-${number}`;
// }
```

A native `RegExp` like `/^ok$/i` is also a valid definition, but infers `string`: TypeScript gives `/…/` literals no type beyond `RegExp`.

## e(x)ec mode

Prefix a regex literal with `x` to validate the string and then parse it into the result of `.exec()`. The definition is a [morph](https://arktype.io/docs/intro/morphs-and-more) from the string to its match:

```ts
const Birthday = type("x/^(?<month>\\d{2})-(?<day>\\d{2})-(?<year>\\d{4})$/")

type Input = typeof Birthday.inferIn
// type Input = `${number}-${number}-${number}`

const match = Birthday.assert("05-21-1993")

const month = match.groups.month
// const month: `${number}`
```

At runtime, `month` is `"05"`.

See [string patterns](https://arktype.io/docs/primitives#string-patterns) for how regex literals fit with ArkType's other string constraints.

# FAQ

> Why some expressions infer string or fail to infer, and the cases ArkRegex currently gets wrong.

## Why is a range like `[a-z]` inferred as `string`?

A range of letters would need a union with a member for every combination of characters, which grows too fast for TypeScript to handle. Digit ranges like `[0-9]` become `` `${number}` `` instead, and small sets like `[abc]` become a union:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

const lower = regex("^[a-z]{3}$")
// const lower: Regex<string, {}>

const abc = regex("^[abc]$")
// const abc: Regex<"a" | "b" | "c", {}>
```

## Which patterns infer the wrong type?

An inferred type is meant to include every string the expression matches. These currently don't:

- `\d` next to an unanchored start or end of a pattern, or followed by `.` or `\w` at the end of a group, infers only `` `${number}` ``. `regex("\\d")` and ArkType's `type("/\\d/")` both infer `` `${number}` ``, but match `"abc1"`.
- A bounded run of more than 308 digits, like `\d{309}`, infers `` `${number}` ``, which can't hold a number that large. An unbounded run like `\d+` infers `string`.
- The `i` flag isn't applied to character sets, and a backreference repeats its group's exact case: `regex("^[ab]$", "i")` infers `"a" | "b"` but matches `"A"`, and `regex("^(a)\\1$", "i")` infers `"aa" | "AA"` but matches `"aA"`.
- The `v` flag's nested classes and set operations, like `[[a-z]--[aeiou]]`, aren't parsed.

`.test()` narrows its input in both branches, so the `false` branch removes strings that didn't match whenever the inferred type was widened:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

const digit = regex("^\\d$")

declare const input: "1" | "12"

if (!digit.test(input)) {
	const rest = input
	// const rest: never
}
```

`"12"` doesn't match, but `"12"` is a `` `${number}` ``, so it's removed. The same happens with the `g` and `y` flags, where `.test()` starts from `lastIndex` and can return `false` for a string that matches.

## Why is my flags string an error?

Flags must be in alphabetical order, the order `RegExp#flags` returns them in. Write `"gi"`, not `"ig"`.

## Why can't it infer my long RegExp?

If your expression is especially long or complex, TypeScript won't be able to infer it. Bounded quantifiers expand into every allowed repetition, so `[ab]{20}` alone produces `Expression produces a union type that is too complex to represent`.

If your types start to slow down or you see an error like that or `Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite`, type the expression yourself with [`regex.as`](https://arktype.io/docs/regex/types#regexas).

## Why does `regex` take a string instead of a `/…/` literal?

TypeScript gives a `/…/` literal the type `RegExp`, with no record of its source, so there's nothing to infer from. A string literal keeps its exact text.

## Are `match`, `replace` and `matchAll` typed?

No. `.test()` and `.exec()` are typed, but string methods like `"abc".match(re)` use TypeScript's standard `RegExp` types.

## How is it tested?

ArkRegex's types are [tested](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/regex/__tests__/regex.test.ts) and [benchmarked](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/blob/main/ark/regex/__tests__/regex.bench.ts) with [Attest](https://arktype.io/docs/attest).

If anything doesn't behave how you'd expect, please [create an issue](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/issues/new).
